analysis.one_liner: Toughens pipeline safety rules with bigger fines, automatic shut-off valves, and more federal inspectors.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late September 2010 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised fines on pipeline operators whose violations cause deaths, injuries, or major environmental damage, required automatic or remote-controlled shut-off valves and excess-flow valves on new pipelines, extended federal safety rules to offshore and Gulf gathering pipelines, added 40 inspectors and staff at the federal pipeline safety agency, and required public disclosure of inspection results. It also funded state damage-prevention programs and set pipeline safety appropriations through 2014.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near gas and hazardous liquid pipelines, including residents of dense neighborhoods crossed by aging gas mains, communities downstream of offshore and gathering pipelines, and emergency responders who would get faster spill notification. Taxpayers also benefit modestly because large pipeline projects would reimburse the government for safety design reviews.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near oil and gas pipelines

how_it_helps.text: Creates a $250,000 civil penalty per 'major consequence violation' — a violation contributing to a death, a hospitalization, over $250,000 in environmental damage, or a dangerous release — with a $2.5 million cap for a related series, and removes 'ability to pay' as a consideration in setting penalties [S2][S3].

Directs the Transportation Secretary to require automatic or remote-controlled shut-off valves on newly constructed pipelines and excess-flow valves on new or replaced branch services, multi-family, and small commercial facilities in high-density and environmentally sensitive areas [S2][S3].
Subjects offshore hazardous liquid gathering pipelines and pipelines within Gulf of Mexico inlets to the same federal standards as other hazardous liquid pipelines, closing a regulatory gap [S2][S3].
Adds 40 full-time employees to the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration for inspections, data collection, and enforcement, subject to appropriations [S2][S3].

Requires monthly public posting of pipeline inspection results, operator facility response plans, and a map of high-consequence areas, and sets time limits for operators to notify state and local officials and emergency responders after a spill or rupture [S2][S3].

Bars state one-call damage-prevention programs (the call-before-you-dig systems) from exempting municipalities, state agencies, and their contractors, and authorizes funding for state damage-prevention and community pipeline safety grants [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators — chiefly oil and gas transmission companies and gas utilities — would bear fines up to $250,000 per serious violation, the cost of installing automatic shut-off and excess-flow valves, leak-detection technology, and expanded reporting. Large pipeline builders (projects over $3.4 billion or 100 miles) would pay the government's design-review costs. Federal spending of roughly $92 million a year for gas pipeline safety plus about $19-20 million for hazardous liquid programs would be appropriated through 2014 [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs — shut-off valves, excess-flow valves, and leak-detection systems on new and replaced pipelines — would be borne by pipeline operators and could be passed through to customers in rates; the bill applies the valve requirements only 'where economically and technically feasible,' acknowledging the cost [S3].

The bill authorizes roughly $112 million a year in federal pipeline safety appropriations through fiscal 2014, adding to federal spending, though state grants require states to maintain their own historic spending levels [S3].

The bill retains and formalizes the waiver system: operators can still obtain exemptions from any pipeline standard for up to five years, renewable, subject to public notice and new factors like the operator's compliance and accident history — a concession that safety advocates might view as leaving a door open [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gains are concrete and targeted: fines that scale with actual harm, valves that stop a rupture from feeding an explosion or spill, inspectors to find problems before they kill, and faster notice to firefighters and residents. The main costs fall on pipeline operators, partly recoverable in rates, and the bill phases requirements in over two years and allows feasibility-based exceptions. The waiver process remains but with more scrutiny. On balance the benefits to communities near pipelines outweigh the costs, though the bill relies on a chronically slow rulemaking process for several of its key protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 28, 2010 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on September 28, 2010, with Senator Jay Rockefeller as the sole cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline operators avoided the higher fines, valve mandates, expanded inspections, and offshore rules; communities near pipelines did not get the added protections this session.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline operators, who avoided new fines and mandates

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; the bill had two Democratic sponsors in the Senate and no recorded opposition appeared in the record before it died in committee.

industries.note: The bill raises penalties for violations that cause deaths, injuries, or major environmental damage, mandates shut-off and excess-flow valves, extends federal rules to offshore and Gulf gathering pipelines, and requires leak detection and public reporting. Operators would absorb these costs, which the bill treats as the price of preventing incidents like ruptures and explosions near homes.

Excess-flow valve requirements and one-call participation rules add compliance costs on new and replaced services, while state grants for damage prevention and clarity on enforcement could reduce third-party excavation damage that utilities otherwise pay to repair.

Projects costing at least $3.4 billion or spanning at least 100 miles would pay the costs of federal design safety reviews and construction oversight into a new Pipeline Safety Design Review Fund, replacing general-taxpayer funding of those reviews.

The bill extends federal safety standards to carbon dioxide pipelines and treats flammable or toxic non-petroleum fuels, including biofuels, as hazardous liquids, bringing previously lightly regulated transport into a formal safety framework.
